image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

raw_comment: After analyzing the graph, I notice that the majority of essential workers are women, with a 52% share. Essential occupations such as resource extraction, farmers, and law enforcement have a majority of men, which may stem from previous social beliefs about occupations for women. One statistic that surprises me is the health care and social care share, which display a majority of women in that field. Even through acts of oppression throughout the 20th century, women are able to receive the majority of essential jobs in our nation, but this doesn’t coordinate with another statistic. Although women take the majority of essential occupations, does their compensation coordinate with their importance in these occupations? Due to previous acts of oppression, it has been an ongoing issue that is still debated. Regardless of the reasoning, women have and will remain an important aspect of the American workforce.

raw_comment: I think this graph is very interesting, and frankly, almost exactly what I would have predicted it to look like. The gender stereotypes I have grown up with and been exposed to are apparent even in the occupational differences between women and men. The medical field and social sciences have always seemed more feminine to me, rather than law enforcement and defense, which appear more predominantly male. I believe a good question to ask ourselves, though, is if this separation of genders in the workplace is inherently bad. Personally, I would argue that no, these differences are not harmful to either gender. They can become detrimental, though, when certain stigmas or stereotypes are enforced because of mere statistics. For example, to say that women only belong in the health fields because they are not capable of anything else, is not only wrong, but also extremely limiting to young girls as they consider their futures. I think that each person should be challenging themselves to think outside of the societal norms that have been in place for decades, encouraging the breakdown of these barriers. No woman, or man, should feel inferior or superior to another simply because of their occupation. I believe it is time to begin challenging the status quo of women in the workforce, encouraging this nation’s young girls to explore their true desires, not those that have been predetermined for them.

- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |
raw_comment: I noticed that women make up a little more than half of the essential worker population. I also noticed that most of the women are social and health care workers. In total, there are 21,410,000 people who hold those jobs and only 16,508,900 are women. It also looks like the percentage of working women decreases from handling medical supplies to resource extraction. I wonder about which states or cities this data came from as well as the pay difference between the men and women who work these jobs. I wonder about how the percentages changed from before the pandemic and how it will be affected once it is over.  Lastly, it’ll be intriguing to learn about the difference in pay for women who are social workers and those who do resource extraction. The impact this topic has on me is quite huge. I am a female, currently in my junior year of high school deciding what career I want to do in the future. This graph opened my eyes to the many essential jobs in the country and gives me an idea of the different careers I can put myself into. The impact this topic has on my community is that there are women within my community who are essential workers. There are also young female adults who are currently looking for jobs or are on their way to pursuing their careers having one of them categorized as essential work. If they choose essential work that is not usually picked up by women, it could change the outlook of jobs that are usually picked up by men.

## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

raw_comment: This graph of the week presents the percentage of essential workers that are female as well as the breakdown of that percentage in each occupation. I notice that there is a higher percentage of women working in white-collar jobs than in blue-collar jobs. Assuming that Social workers, Health care, Medical supplies, and Financial IT are all white-collar jobs and the rest are blue-collar and that the numbers in the middle were the percent of women in the job, then 75.59% of the 22,290,000 white-collar workers, are women. However, women only hold 31.09% of 26,500,000 blue-collar jobs. 

I also noticed that when you add up all of the total workers on the right side of the graph, they equal 48,790,000, as opposed to the 48,710,000 that are all the essential workers. I thought that maybe the percent of total essential workers that are women would be different, but after finding the amount of women for all of the individual types of jobs and then adding them up and dividing them by the total number of workers, I got 52% which was what the graph had originally said. 

I wonder where the extra 80,000 workers came from when adding the number of workers on the right. 
I wonder why there are more women in white-collar jobs than in blue-collar.
Lastly, I wonder how accurate these numbers are today, and how much they have changed from this 2014-2018 survey.

I think this graph could be called: "Are Essential jobs need Essential Woman."

raw_comment: I notice that the number of women that are essential workers is slightly above half, but that only 3 of the jobs were greater than 50% (social workers health care workers, and critical retail workers). ## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal bar chart / progress-bar style chart**
- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.
- **No faceting** or small multiples.
- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

At the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic, the Department of Homeland Security designated which job categories were essential.  These workers should be going to their jobs.  Today’s graph shows the share of “essential workers” who are women.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “What impact does this topic have on you and your community?”  Then, please share a catchy headline that captures the idea in the graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.
Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”

- Each row shows the **share who are women** as a filled horizontal bar, with a numeric label inside the bar and a separate right-aligned number for **total workers**.

- **Single-panel ranked list** of categories.

- Uses **aligned horizontal bars** by category.
- The bars are effectively **part-to-whole/progress bars**: purple filled portion for the women’s share against a light gray full-length background.
- A horizontal divider separates **“All essential workers”** from the occupation-specific rows.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Occupation / worker group (e.g., Social workers, Health care, Critical retail, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Row position; left-side text labels |
| Share who are women (%) | Quantitative | Horizontal bar length (purple fill); numeric text label inside bar |
| Total workers | Quantitative | Right-side numeric text label |
| All essential workers vs. specific occupations | Categorical/nominal | Separate row placement; horizontal divider indicating grouping |

raw_comment: I notice that while 52% of essential workers are women, men dominate more than 75% of the fields. Women completely dominate 78% of social work and 77% health care. However, the number of women drop in the other fields where they are greatly dominated by men, such as defense, law enforcement, farmers, and IT services. I wonder if this is due to hiring practices or a belief held by women that they can't pursue careers in these fields. This also can be a sign that men aren't as encouraged to pursue careers in the non-doctoral (?) medicine and caring fields as women are. I also wonder if the graph is misleading. The graph shows how many of the workers in that field are women but doesn't really include data about the total number. With differing sizes in workforces for different fields, the data may be interpreted differently with more information added. I also am not sure if the "Total Workers" column to the right refers to the number of women or actual total including men, which could help answer my previous question. This impacts me and my community because it can inform us of the disparities between different genders in different fields. School and human resource programs can use this information to level the playing field and encourage more men and women to join fields not dominated by their genders. A possible catchy headline is "Women Dominate Essential Workers...or do they?" or "Essential Workers: Are both genders essential?"

I noticed that although out of the total number of essential workers women only take up 4% more than men, the data is extremely varied across all occupations, ranging from 11% in resource extraction to 78% of social workers. Personally, I was shocked when I also noticed that women constitute 77% of the healthcare workforce, which is nearly 40% of all essential occupations.
	I wonder why teaching and education have not been included in the essential works list, and if they were, what would the share of women in that area be? Would that data entry drive the average percentage of women in the essential workforce upwards? If yes, that (alongside their share in healthcare) would once again show us just how incredibly important women’s jobs really are and the degree to which our entire society relies on them.
	At the moment, this particular topic has a tremendous impact on the entire nation, including me and the community in which we live. In a time when the majority of the workforce is slowly just starting to come back to work, it is the essential workers who have been carrying all of us on their backs by working on the frontlines in spite of all the risks — the vast majority of them were women. Now, it is our responsibility to remember their effort and be thankful for their unconditional desire to help everyone else.
	Finally, a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea would be “Who are our frontline workers?”
